questions.question: With dplyr loaded, `filter(d, Year = 2021)` stops with an error, although the tibble `d` has a numeric column `Year`. Why?
options: A single `=` would overwrite `Year` with 2021, and `filter()` may not change columns.
Column names inside `filter()` must be quoted, as in `filter(d, "Year" == 2021)`.
A single `=` names an argument, while keeping rows needs the comparison `==`.
`Year` holds doubles, so the condition must use the integer `2021L` instead.

questions.question: A tibble `d` with numeric columns `x` and `y` has 50 rows. Which call can return a tibble with fewer than 50 rows?

With dplyr loaded and `d <- tibble(x = c(4, NA, 1, 7))`, what does `d %>% filter(x > 2) %>% pull(x)` return?
With dplyr loaded, what does `tibble(x = c(3, NA, 8, 5)) %>% arrange(desc(x)) %>% pull(x)` return?
With dplyr loaded, a tibble `d` has the columns `old_price` and `qty`. Which call returns a tibble with exactly the columns `price` and `qty`?
With dplyr loaded and `d <- tibble(city = c("A", "A", "B", "B", "B"), year = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 2))`, what does `d %>% distinct(city, year) %>% nrow()` return?
With dplyr loaded, what does R print at the end of `d <- tibble(a = c(1, 2), b = c(3, 4)); d %>% mutate(s = a + b); names(d)`?
With dplyr loaded, `d <- tibble(p = c(10, 20), q = c(1, 2))`. What does `d %>% mutate(p = p * q)` return?
options: Two columns, `p` and `q`, with `p` now equal to `10 40`.
Three columns: the old `p`, `q`, and a new `p` equal to `10 40`.
Two columns, with `p` still `10 20`, as `p` cannot be defined from itself.
An error, since a column with the name `p` already exists in `d`.

questions.question: With dplyr loaded and `d <- tibble(x = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9), y = c("a", "a", "b", "a", "b"))`, what does `d %>% filter(x > 2, y == "a") %>% nrow()` return?
A tibble `d` has the columns `Country`, `Year` and `Transport`. Why does `d %>% select(Country, Transport) %>% filter(Year == 2021)` stop with the error `object 'Year' not found`?
options: dplyr requires `filter()` to come before `select()` in every pipe, and enforces it.
`filter()` receives the output of `select()`, which no longer has a `Year` column.
`select()` returns a vector rather than a tibble, so `filter()` finds no columns at all.
`select()` removed `Year` from `d` itself, so the column is gone for good.

questions.question: With dplyr loaded and `d <- tibble(city = c("A", "A", "B"), year = c(1, 2, 1), sales = c(5, 6, 7))`, what does `distinct(d, city)` return?
options: A tibble with 3 rows and all three columns, as no row repeats in full.
A tibble with 2 rows and all three columns: the first row per city.
The character vector `"A" "B"`, the distinct cities only.
A tibble with 2 rows and the single column `city`.

options: an error, because `mean(x)` has length 1 while `x` has length 3

questions.question: With dplyr loaded, what does `tibble(g = c("b", "a", "b", "a"), v = c(1, 4, 3, 2)) %>% arrange(g, desc(v)) %>% pull(v)` return?
A data frame `d` has `x = c(4, NA, 1)` and `y = c("p", "q", "r")`. Compare dplyr's `filter(d, x > 2)` with base R's `d[d[["x"]] > 2, ]`. How do the two results differ?
options: They are identical: both return only the row with `x` equal to 4.
`filter()` keeps the row whose `x` is `NA`; base R drops that row.
`filter()` returns one row; base R adds a second row filled with `NA`.
Both return two rows: the row with `x` equal to 4 and the `NA` row.

questions.question: With dplyr loaded and `d <- tibble(country = c("NL", "NL", "BE", "BE"), v = c(1, 2, 3, 4))`, what does `d %>% filter(country == c("NL", "BE")) %>% pull(v)` return?
options: an error, since `c("NL", "BE")` has 2 elements and `country` has 4
